title: Wahlund effect in 1000 Genomes
question: Per variant and pooled sample (ALL, each super-population), is the observed heterozygote deficit F explained by F_ST, the variance of the pooled populations' allele frequencies over p̄(1 − p̄)?

hypotheses.statement: In pooled samples the heterozygote deficit F rises one for one with F_ST predicted from the populations' allele frequencies.
hypotheses.null: F in pooled samples is unrelated to F_ST (pooling does not explain the departures).

hypotheses.statement: Within single populations the genotypes follow Hardy–Weinberg: F is near 0 and p < 0.05 no more often than chance (5%).
hypotheses.null: Single populations depart from Hardy–Weinberg more often than chance.

hypotheses.statement: The sickle-cell allele (rs334) has more heterozygotes than Hardy–Weinberg expects in African populations (F < 0): HbS homozygotes are rare because sickle-cell disease is severe, while carriers are protected from malaria.
hypotheses.null: rs334 genotypes in African populations follow Hardy–Weinberg (F = 0).

concepts.label: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium
concepts.description: Genotype frequencies p², 2pq, q² under random mating.
concepts.why: The null model each sample is tested against.

concepts.label: Population differentiation (F_ST)
concepts.description: Variance of allele frequency between populations over p̄(1 − p̄).

concepts.label: Natural selection
concepts.description: Selection on the variant (lactase persistence, skin colour, malaria resistance).
concepts.why: Drives the frequency differences behind F_ST, and for HbS the heterozygote excess.

strategy.detail: Selection scans (e.g. iHS, PBS) per variant from the literature or Ensembl's variant pages.

issues.text: Five variants and six pooled samples per variant give 30 points for H1; populations of about 100 people have little power to see small departures within populations.
issues.fix: Read H2 as 'no large departures'; add variants (any rsID works) to widen H1.

issues.text: Departures from Hardy–Weinberg can also come from genotyping errors, relatives in the sample or selection, not only pooling.
issues.fix: H1 says how much pooling explains; the gap column holds the rest.

alternatives.question: Does the pooled deficit in each super-population match F_ST among its own populations?
alternatives.why: Drill down: the same law at a finer scale.

alternatives.question: Do variants under known selection (LCT, SLC24A5) have higher F_ST than random common variants?
alternatives.why: Expand: needs a sample of random variants.

data.request: Genotype counts per 1000 Genomes population for a random sample of common SNPs (MAF > 5%).

method.summary: Regress F_observed on fst across the 30 pooled samples (5 variants × ALL and 5 super-populations); Wahlund predicts slope 1 and intercept 0.

steps.title: Hardy–Weinberg per sample
steps.detail: hwe: p, expected counts, chi2 (1 df), p_value and F per variant and sample.

steps.title: F_ST from the populations
steps.detail: wahlund: size-weighted variance of p among the populations pooled, over p̄(1 − p̄).

steps.title: Regress F_observed on fst
steps.detail: 30 rows of wahlund; read the slope against 1.

steps.title: Pooling or something else?
steps.detail: Accept H1 when the slope is near 1; read gap = F_observed − fst for what pooling leaves; check H3 on rs334's African rows of hwe.

caveats: The five variants were chosen because they are known to differ between populations or be under selection: they are not a random sample.
1000 Genomes populations have about 60–113 people: a population chi-square has little power, and rare genotypes make it unreliable (expected counts under 5).
Genotypes are imputed and phased calls, not direct assays; errors show as departures from Hardy–Weinberg too.
F_ST here is the simple variance ratio over the populations pooled (no sample-size correction, as in Weir & Cockerham).
